evidence.claim: briefly turns inland through redwoods in the Big Sur River valley.

evidence.claim: The Big Sur coast became California’s first State Scenic Highway in 1965; the San Luis Obispo-to-Carmel section has National Scenic Byway status.
evidence.quote: The section of road along the Big Sur Coast was declared the first State Scenic Highway in 1965

evidence.claim: the San Luis Obispo-to-Carmel section has National Scenic Byway status.
evidence.quote: The Big Sur section from San Luis Obispo to Carmel is an official National Scenic Byway.

evidence.claim: The highway came together in sections. In 1919, California approved the Carmel-San Simeon Highway to connect Big Sur with the rest of the state.
evidence.quote: The state first approved building Route 56, or the Carmel-San Simeon Highway, to connect Big Sur to the rest of California in 1919.

evidence.claim: The highway came together in sections.
evidence.quote: SR 1 was built piecemeal in various stages

evidence.claim: San Quentin established prison camps whose incarcerated workers helped build the road.
evidence.quote: San Quentin State Prison set up three temporary prison camps to provide unskilled convict labor to help with road construction.

evidence.claim: Workers received 35 cents a day and sentence reductions.
evidence.quote: Inmates were paid 35 cents per day and had their prison sentences reduced in return.

evidence.claim: The route required 33 bridges and opened on June 17, 1937, after 18 years of construction.
evidence.quote: The route necessitated construction of 33 bridges

evidence.claim: opened on June 17, 1937, after 18 years of construction.
evidence.quote: After 18 years of construction, aided by New Deal funds during the Great Depression, the paved two-lane road was completed and opened on June 17, 1937.

evidence.claim: The full route acquired its unified SR 1 designation in the 1964 renumbering.
evidence.quote: It was not until the 1964 state highway renumbering that the entire route was officially designated as SR 1.

evidence.claim: Southbound from US 101 near Leggett, follow Cottaneva Creek through redwood country toward the coast.
evidence.quote: The highway follows Cottaneva Creek inland through redwood-forested mountainous terrain before terminating at US 101 just outside Leggett.

evidence.claim: Route 1 becomes Main Street in Fort Bragg.
evidence.quote: becomes Main Street of Fort Bragg

evidence.claim: Farther south, cross the Golden Gate Bridge with US 101.
evidence.quote: through a short stretch of northern San Francisco and southern Marin County that includes  the Golden Gate Bridge.

evidence.claim: Continue through Davenport, Santa Cruz and Monterey toward Big Sur.
evidence.quote: continues north-west as a two-lane road (with occasional four-lane sections) up the coast through Davenport.

evidence.claim: Continue through Davenport, Santa Cruz and Monterey toward Big Sur.
evidence.quote: CA 1, also known as the Cabrillo Highway, as it runs along the coastline of the rest of Monterey Bay to the north and Big Sur to the south.

evidence.claim: Beyond San Simeon, the route reaches San Luis Obispo, turns inland through parts of the Central Coast and shares US 101 through Santa Barbara.
evidence.quote: The US 101/SR 1 concurrency (although actual signage mentioning SR 1 through this segment is nonexistent) from the Mobil Pier Undercrossing runs for 54 miles (87 km), passing through the City of Santa Barbara

evidence.claim: Beyond San Simeon, the route reaches San Luis Obispo
evidence.quote: Route 56 was extended further south from Cambria to connect to present-day US 101 in San Luis Obispo in 1931.

evidence.claim: turns inland through parts of the Central Coast
evidence.quote: The US 101/SR 1 concurrency then avoids the immediate coastline of Avila Beach and Diablo Canyon Power Plant, and instead heads straight inland to San Luis Obispo.

evidence.claim: It follows the Malibu coast, crosses the Los Angeles area and continues through Orange County to I-5 at Dana Point.
evidence.quote: At its southernmost end in Orange County, SR 1 terminates at I-5 in Capistrano Beach in Dana Point.

evidence.claim: It follows the Malibu coast, crosses the Los Angeles area
evidence.quote: PCH continues to follow the coast, curving west through the Pacific Palisades neighborhood of Los Angeles before becoming the main thoroughfare of the city of Malibu

evidence.claim: Glass Beach began as a dumping ground on the edge of Fort Bragg.
evidence.quote: Glass Beach is on the edge of Fort Bragg, along the ocean.

evidence.claim: In the early twentieth century, residents threw household rubbish over Union Lumber Company cliffs, including glass, appliances and vehicles.
evidence.quote: In the early 20th century, Fort Bragg residents threw their household garbage over cliffs owned by the Union Lumber Company onto what is now Glass Beach, discarding glass, appliances, and even vehicles.

evidence.claim: City leaders closed the dump in 1967, and cleanup programs followed.
evidence.quote: In 1967, city leaders closed the area and various cleanup programs were brought on through the years to fix the damage.

evidence.claim: Over decades, waves worked the discarded glass into small, smooth pieces of sea glass.
evidence.quote: Over several decades the pounding waves wore down the discarded glass into the small, smooth pieces called sea glass

evidence.claim: Through town, Route 1 carries the name Main Street and crosses both the Noyo River and Pudding Creek on bridges.
evidence.quote: State Route 1 (the Pacific Coast Highway) passes through Fort Bragg, concurrent with and signed as Main Street within the city limits. It travels on two bridges while doing so, the Noyo River Bridge and the Pudding Creek Bridge.

evidence.claim: The beach at the end of Elm Street became a destination for visitors to the coast.
evidence.quote: The area along the beach at the end of Elm Street is now visited by tourists.

evidence.claim: Davenport’s name traveled from a lumber landing to a cement town.
evidence.quote: It again only used the name of Davenport; hence, the name of the town.

evidence.claim: Captain John Pope Davenport built a 400-foot wharf at Agua Puerca Creek to load lumber brought down from the hills.
evidence.quote: Davenport built a 400-foot wharf at the mouth of Agua Puerca Creek ("agua puerca" translates to "muddy water"). This wharf was built to load the lumber brought down from the hills for shipment to Santa Cruz.

evidence.claim: Mud filled the port until steamers could no longer reach the wharf, and an extension failed to solve the problem.
evidence.quote: Agua Puerca Creek lived up to its name by bringing down so much mud that the port filled up and steamers could not tie up to the wharf to load lumber. A small extension did not solve the problem.

evidence.claim: After the Santa Cruz Portland Cement Company plant was built in 1906, the post office reopened in the settlement beside it, carrying the Davenport name to the new town.
evidence.quote: In the following year, the Santa Cruz Portland Cement Company manufacturing plant was built nearby. At that time, the closed Davenport Landing post office opened up in the settlement that grew up around the cement plant. It again only used the name of Davenport; hence, the name of the town.

evidence.claim: plant was built in 1906
evidence.quote: The cement plant was built in 1906

evidence.claim: The cement plant ceased operations in 2010; its remains lie north of the town’s homes.
evidence.quote: The remains of a closed cement plant, last operated by Cemex in 2010, lie just north of the small concentration of homes in Davenport.

evidence.claim: Lucia sits 22 miles south of Big Sur Village in a sparsely settled part of the coast.
evidence.quote: Lucia is a hamlet located 22 miles (35 km) south of Big Sur Village and 38 miles (61 km) north of Hearst Castle in Monterey County, California, United States. The area is sparsely settled.

evidence.claim: Before the coast highway was completed, travelers used Wagon Cave as a resting place between the coast and inland markets.
evidence.quote: Before the completion of the coast highway, Wagon Cave was used as a resting point and overnight camp site for those traveling to and from the coast.

evidence.claim: They changed from horseback to wagons kept there, then followed an 18-mile wagon road to Jolon for goods and supplies.
evidence.quote: Travelers on horseback switched to wagons stored there for the purpose of transporting goods to market and provisions home. From the Caves there was a 18 miles (29 km) wagon road to Jolon.

evidence.claim: The store at Lucia opened in 1937, the same year the Big Sur Coast Highway opened.
evidence.quote: In 1937, the Lucia store opened coinciding with the opening of Big Sur Coast Highway.

evidence.claim: The modern highway has its own adaptations to the terrain: south of Lucia, a bridge and covered rock shed replaced the landslide-prone section at Pitkins Curve and Rain Rocks.
evidence.quote: A section south of Lucia that is also prone to frequent landslides, known as Pitkins Curve and Rain Rocks, was replaced with a bridge and a covered rock shed.

evidence.claim: Landslides and coastal erosion have repeatedly closed sections of Route 1 for long periods.
evidence.quote: Frequent landslides and erosion along the coast have caused portions of SR 1 to either be closed for long periods of time, or be re-routed entirely.

evidence.claim: Dana Point’s harbor changed both the anchorage and the surf.
evidence.quote: The break was destroyed by a  breakwater built when the construction of Dana Point Harbor in 1966.

evidence.claim: The harbor was built in the 1960s and dedicated on July 31, 1971.
evidence.quote: The harbor, built in the 1960s and dedicated on July 31, 1971

evidence.claim: Construction of its breakwater destroyed the surf break called Killer Dana, which had risen from deep water and broken near the shoreline rocks.
evidence.quote: "Killer Dana" was a notorious surf break off Dana Point that came out of deep water and broke close to the rocks that lined the beach. The break was destroyed by a  breakwater built when the construction of Dana Point Harbor in 1966.

evidence.claim: The city’s name comes from Richard Henry Dana Jr., whose 1840 memoir, Two Years Before the Mast, described the area.
evidence.quote: The city was named after the headland of Dana Point, which was in turn named after Richard Henry Dana Jr., whose 1840 memoir Two Years Before the Mast included a description of the area.

evidence.claim: Dana visited in 1835 aboard the brig Pilgrim, during the coast’s hide-trading era.
evidence.quote: Richard Henry Dana then visited the area in 1835 while serving aboard the sailing brig Pilgrim on her voyage along the California coastline.

evidence.claim: during the coast’s hide-trading era.
evidence.quote: Dana Point was a popular port for ships involved with the hide trade with nearby Mission San Juan Capistrano. Trading reached its peak in the 1830s and 1840s.

evidence.claim: Route 1 reaches its southern end here, meeting I-5 in Capistrano Beach.
evidence.quote: At its southernmost end in Orange County, SR 1 terminates at I-5 in Capistrano Beach in Dana Point.

flags: All California cache pages are secondary sources. No Caltrans or byway-body page substantiates a designation rationale or current access. Scenic designations are limited to the specifically documented sections; the cache’s broader All-American Road wording is not generalized to the whole route.
Catalog mapped length is 735 miles; highway page gives 656 miles. Omitted total mileage because the corridor geometry and numbered-highway scope differ.

No current closure status can be established. The cache mixes historical closures with an assertion that a Lucia closure lasted until January 2026; neither an open-through claim nor a present closure is made.

Current Lucia cabin count, cliff height and refusal-to-sell story have cache support but were replaced with the town’s transport history to avoid making a lodging business the subject. The Harlan family chronology is internally inconsistent and is omitted.
Current Fort Bragg text specifically said bottles; cache says glass, appliances and vehicles, so bottles is dropped.
No story-level motifs were present in current; empty array supplied.
Pasatiempo’s strip mile is inconsistent with the north-to-south sequence and its cache places it on Route 17; omitted.
Prison-labor details are supported only by the highway secondary source; no archival or agency history is cached.
The dated Lucia practical note records a cache check of the documented recurring road disruption, not live closure verification or a current detour.
